learn.hook: Electrostatics froze charges in place. Now let them flow, and you get everything from a lightning bolt to the UPI payment pinging on your phone.
points: Moving charges make an electric current. Examples: lightning in a thunderstorm, electrons in battery circuits, ions in electrolytes and in our nerves.
Current I = rate of flow of charge. Steady current: I = q/t. In general I(t) = dq/dt, the limit of Δq/Δt.
SI unit: ampere (A), a base unit; 1 A = 1 C s⁻¹. Smaller units: mA (10⁻³ A) and µA (10⁻⁶ A).
Conventional current is the direction of flow of positive charge, so it is opposite to the flow of electrons.
Typical sizes: household appliances draw a few amperes, nerve signals involve microamperes, while lightning can carry tens of thousands of amperes.

example.q: A charge of 360 C passes through a heater coil in 3 minutes. Find the current.

learn.reallife: Your phone charger's label says, for example, 5 V, 2 A. That 2 A means 2 coulombs of charge flow into the battery every second when charging at full speed.

topics.title: Charge flow in conductors and Ohm's law

learn.hook: Inside a copper wire, electrons zip around at about 10⁶ m s⁻¹, yet without a battery no current flows. Why? Their motion is random.
points: Charge carriers: free electrons in metals; positive and negative ions in electrolytes.
With no field, free electrons move randomly in all directions, so the net flow through any cross-section is zero.
A field applied across the conductor gives electrons a small net drift, producing a current. A cell or other source is needed to keep the field going, or charges would pile up and cancel it.
Ohm's law: for a metallic conductor at constant temperature, V ∝ I, so V = IR. R is the resistance, unit ohm (Ω), 1 Ω = 1 V A⁻¹.
A graph of V against I for an ohmic conductor is a straight line through the origin; its slope is R.

example.q: A 12 V source drives 0.4 A through a resistor. Find R and the current if V is raised to 18 V (same temperature).

learn.reallife: An electrician testing a geyser element in a Pune flat uses a multimeter: measuring V and I and dividing gives R, exactly Ohm's law.

learn.hook: Why are Indian Railways' overhead lines thick copper alloy, while a geyser element is thin nichrome? It comes down to R = ρl/A.
points: R = ρl/A: resistance is proportional to length l and inversely proportional to cross-sectional area A.
Resistivity ρ is a property of the material (and temperature), not of the shape. Unit: Ω m. Copper has ρ ≈ 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m.
Conductivity σ = 1/ρ, unit S m⁻¹ (siemens per metre) or Ω⁻¹ m⁻¹.
Current density j = I/A (A m⁻²), and Ohm's law in vector form is j = σE.
Stretching a wire keeps its volume constant: if length becomes n times, area becomes 1/n times, so R becomes n² times.

example.q: A wire of resistance 4 Ω is stretched to twice its length. Find the new resistance.
steps: Volume is constant: l → 2l, A → A/2

learn.reallife: Copper or aluminium is used for transmission lines in India because their low ρ keeps losses down. Nichrome, with high ρ, is chosen for heaters and irons.

topics.title: Drift velocity and the origin of resistance

learn.hook: Electrons in your house wiring crawl at less than a millimetre per second, yet the bulb lights the instant you flip the switch. Both facts are true at once.
points: In a field E, each free electron accelerates (a = -eE/m) between collisions; the average time between collisions is the relaxation time τ.
Drift velocity: vd = -eEτ/m, the average velocity of electrons, opposite to E.
Current I = neAvd, where n is the number density of free electrons and A is the cross-section.
Combining, j = (ne²τ/m)E, so ρ = m/(ne²τ). Resistance arises from collisions.
vd is tiny (about 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹), but the field travels along the wire nearly at the speed of light, so all electrons start drifting almost at once.

example.q: A copper wire (n = 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³) of cross-section 10⁻⁶ m² carries 1.36 A. Find vd.

learn.reallife: An Indian Railways signal kilometres away responds instantly when the cabin switch is thrown, even though electrons in the cable barely creep. The field, not the individual electron, carries the signal.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'If electrons are so slow, how does my lamp light up instantly?'

revise.summary: Electrons accelerate in a field between collisions with average relaxation time τ, giving drift velocity vd = −eEτ/m. Current I = neAvd and resistivity ρ = m/(ne²τ); drift is slow but the field spreads almost instantly.
traps: A bulb lights at once because the field travels fast, not the electrons

learn.hook: Ohm's law is not a law of nature like gravity; it is a rule many materials obey. Diodes, LEDs and even a hot bulb filament break it.
points: Mobility µ = |vd|/E = eτ/m: drift speed per unit field. SI unit: m² V⁻¹ s⁻¹.
Non-ohmic case 1: the V-I graph is not a straight line, for example a bulb filament whose resistance rises as it heats up at high currents.
Non-ohmic case 2: the relation depends on the sign of V, as in a diode, which conducts much more in one direction.
Non-ohmic case 3: more than one value of V for the same I, as shown by GaAs-type materials.
For non-ohmic devices, V/I is not constant, so a single resistance value does not describe them.

example.q: Electrons drift at 2 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹ in a field of 0.04 V m⁻¹. Find their mobility.

learn.reallife: The LED strings used for Diwali lights are non-ohmic devices: they barely conduct until a threshold voltage, and only in one direction.

Diode: depends on sign of V; GaAs: one I, many V

topics.title: Resistivity of materials and its temperature dependence

learn.hook: From silver to quartz, resistivities span more than 20 orders of magnitude, the biggest range of any common physical property.
points: Materials are classified by resistivity: conductors (metals, about 10⁻⁸ to 10⁻⁶ Ω m), semiconductors (in between) and insulators (up to 10¹⁴ Ω m or more).
The range covers more than 20 orders of magnitude.
For metals, ρ rises with temperature: ρT = ρ₀[1 + α(T - T₀)], where α is the temperature coefficient of resistivity (unit K⁻¹ or °C⁻¹).
For metals α is positive. Alloys like manganin and constantan have very small α, so they are used for standard resistors.
Nichrome has high ρ and small α, so it is used in heating elements.

example.q: A wire has R = 20 Ω at 20 °C and α = 4 × 10⁻³ °C⁻¹. Find R at 70 °C.

learn.reallife: Standard resistors at India's National Physical Laboratory in New Delhi are made from alloys like manganin, whose resistance barely changes with room temperature.

quiz.q: Why is nichrome preferred for the heating coil of an electric iron?
options: It has high resistivity and its resistance changes little when hot
quiz.explain: High ρ gives large R in a short coil; small α keeps the heating steady.
steps: High ρ gives large resistance in a short coil
Small α keeps the resistance steady when hot
Answer: It has high resistivity and its resistance changes little when hot
quiz.mistake: Thinks a heater needs very low resistivity

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why does a metal wire resist more when it gets hot?'
teach.praise: Chirp! For metals, resistivity rises with temperature: ρ = ρ₀[1 + α(T - T₀)] with positive α. Nice!
teach.nudge: Good! How does the resistivity of a metal depend on temperature?

revise.summary: Resistivity ranges from about 10⁻⁸ Ω m for metals to 10¹⁴ Ω m for insulators, with semiconductors between. For metals ρ rises with temperature as ρT = ρ₀[1 + α(T − T₀)]; manganin and constantan have tiny α and nichrome suits heaters.
remember: Manganin, constantan: tiny α (standard resistors); nichrome: high ρ, small α (heaters)
traps: Use T − T₀, not T alone
Semiconductors' resistivity does not behave like metals'

learn.hook: Heat a copper wire and it resists more. Heat a silicon chip and it conducts better. One formula, ρ = m/(ne²τ), explains both.
points: Semiconductors and insulators: resistivity decreases as temperature rises (negative α).
Using ρ = m/(ne²τ): in metals, n is nearly constant, but hotter ions vibrate more, collisions are more frequent, τ falls, so ρ rises.
In semiconductors, extra heat frees many more charge carriers; the rise in n outweighs the fall in τ, so ρ falls.
Finding the temperature of a heating element: from R and R₀ and α, use T = T₀ + (R - R₀)/(R₀α).
This principle is used in resistance thermometers and in thermistors.

example.q: A heating element has R = 60 Ω at 25 °C (from V/I) and 69 Ω when hot. With α = 1.5 × 10⁻⁴ °C⁻¹, find the hot temperature.

learn.reallife: Digital thermometers used in Indian clinics often contain a thermistor, a semiconductor whose resistance falls sharply as body heat warms it.

games.title: Metal or semiconductor behaviour?
items: ρ rises with temperature
ρ falls with temperature
n almost constant with temperature
n rises sharply with temperature
Positive α
Negative α

quiz.q: Why does the resistivity of a metal increase with temperature?
options: The number of free electrons drops sharply
Collisions become more frequent, so the relaxation time τ decreases
quiz.explain: In ρ = m/(ne²τ), n stays almost constant while τ falls.
steps: ρ = m/(ne²τ); in metals n stays nearly constant
Hotter ions vibrate more, collisions are more frequent, τ falls
Answer: Collisions become more frequent, so the relaxation time τ decreases
quiz.mistake: Thinks the number of free electrons falls

quiz.q: Why does the resistivity of a semiconductor decrease with temperature?
options: The relaxation time increases a lot
The number density of charge carriers increases rapidly
The mass of the electron decreases
quiz.explain: More bonds break, freeing carriers; this beats the drop in τ.
steps: In semiconductors heat frees many more charge carriers
The rise in n outweighs the fall in τ, so ρ falls
Answer: The number density of charge carriers increases rapidly
quiz.mistake: Thinks semiconductors behave like metals

quiz.q: A heater coil has R = 100 Ω at 20 °C and 120 Ω when hot, with α = 2 × 10⁻⁴ °C⁻¹. What is its hot temperature (in °C)?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to add the starting temperature

quiz.q: The temperature coefficient of resistivity of a semiconductor is
options: always equal to that of copper
quiz.explain: Its resistivity falls as temperature rises.
steps: Semiconductor resistivity falls as temperature rises
So its temperature coefficient α is negative
quiz.mistake: Assumes all materials resist more when hot

quiz.q: In the expression ρ = m/(ne²τ), which quantity changes most with temperature in a metal?
quiz.explain: n is fixed by the metal's structure; τ falls as lattice vibrations grow.
steps: In ρ = m/(ne²τ), m and e are constants; n is nearly fixed in a metal
τ falls as lattice vibrations grow
quiz.mistake: Thinks n changes in metals

quiz.q: A platinum resistance thermometer reads 5 Ω at 0 °C and 6 Ω at an unknown temperature. If α = 4 × 10⁻³ °C⁻¹, what is the temperature (in °C)?
quiz.mistake: Divides by the final resistance

quiz.q: Assertion (A): An insulator's resistivity decreases with increasing temperature. Reason (R): More charge carriers become available as temperature rises. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
quiz.explain: Like semiconductors, heating frees a few carriers in insulators, lowering resistivity.
steps: A: insulator resistivity falls with temperature – true
R: more carriers become available as temperature rises – true
More carriers is the cause, so R explains A
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks only metals depend on temperature

quiz.q: Which statement correctly compares heating a copper wire and a silicon crystal?
options: Copper's resistance rises while silicon's falls
quiz.explain: Metals have positive α; semiconductors have negative α.
steps: Copper (metal): α > 0, resistance rises when heated
Answer: Copper's resistance rises while silicon's falls
quiz.mistake: Gives the same trend for both

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Copper resists more when hot, silicon resists less. Who is lying?'
teach.praise: Chirp! In metals τ drops as collisions increase; in semiconductors many more carriers appear. Nobody lies!
teach.nudge: Good! Use ρ = m/(ne²τ). Which factor changes in a metal, and which in a semiconductor?

revise.summary: In metals n is fixed and hotter ions shorten τ, so resistivity rises; in semiconductors and insulators heat frees many carriers, so resistivity falls. The hot temperature of an element follows from T = T₀ + (R − R₀)/(R₀α).
traps: ΔT is not the final temperature; add it to T₀
In metals n does not change much with temperature

learn.hook: Your electricity bill counts kilowatt-hours, and every one of them comes from charges falling through potential differences, warming wires on the way.
points: When charge q moves through potential difference V, energy qV is delivered. Power P = VI.
For a resistor, P = VI = I²R = V²/R. This energy appears as heat (Joule heating).
Transmission lines lose power I²Rc in their resistance Rc.
To deliver power P at voltage V, I = P/V, so loss = P²Rc/V². Raising V greatly reduces the loss.
That is why power is sent at very high voltages (hundreds of kV) and stepped down near homes.

example.q: A 1000 W heater runs on 220 V. Find the current and resistance.

learn.reallife: POWERGRID runs 765 kV lines across India so that the current, and hence I²R loss, stays small over thousands of kilometres.

games.title: Power facts
items: Joule heating in a resistor equals I²R per second.
P = I²R.
Sending power at higher voltage increases the current in the line.
For fixed P, higher V means lower I.
The power lost in a line is proportional to the square of the current.
Loss = I²R.
A 100 W bulb has more resistance than a 60 W bulb at the same voltage.
R = V²/P, so the 100 W bulb has less resistance.

quiz.q: A resistor of 10 Ω carries 3 A. What power does it dissipate (in W)?
quiz.mistake: Uses P = IR

quiz.q: A 60 W bulb is designed for 240 V. What is its resistance (in Ω)?
quiz.mistake: Divides V by P

quiz.q: A 2 kW geyser runs for 30 minutes a day. How many kWh does it use in 30 days?
quiz.explain: Daily: 2 kW × 0.5 h = 1 kWh. In 30 days: 30 kWh.
quiz.mistake: Uses minutes instead of hours

quiz.q: A power of 100 kW is sent through a line of resistance 0.5 Ω at 10 kV. What is the power lost in the line (in W)?
quiz.mistake: Uses V²/R with the supply voltage, which is not the voltage across the line

quiz.q: If the same 100 kW is sent through the same 0.5 Ω line at 100 kV instead, what is the loss (in W)?
quiz.explain: I = 1 A, loss = 1 × 0.5 = 0.5 W, a hundredth of the earlier loss.
quiz.mistake: Thinks loss falls only ten times when V rises ten times

quiz.q: Why is electric power transmitted at very high voltage?
options: Wires have zero resistance at high voltage
For a given power, higher V means lower current and much smaller I²R loss
High voltage is safer for homes
quiz.explain: Loss = P²Rc/V² falls as 1/V².
steps: Line loss = I²Rc = P²Rc/V², which falls as 1/V²
Answer: For a given power, higher V means lower current and much smaller I²R loss
quiz.mistake: Thinks high voltage itself reduces resistance

quiz.q: Two bulbs of 40 W and 100 W, both rated for 220 V, are connected in series across 220 V. Which glows brighter?
quiz.explain: In series the same current flows, so P = I²R is larger for the larger R. The 40 W bulb has the higher resistance (R = V²/P).
steps: R = V²/P: the 40 W bulb has the larger resistance
In series the same current flows, so P = I²R is larger for larger R
quiz.mistake: Assumes the higher rated bulb always glows brighter

quiz.q: A 5 Ω resistor is connected across 10 V. How much heat is produced in 1 minute (in J)?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to convert 1 minute into 60 s

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why are power lines at lakhs of volts? Isn't that dangerous and wasteful?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Higher voltage means smaller current for the same power, so I²R loss is tiny. Efficient!
teach.nudge: Good! For the same power, how does raising the voltage change the current and the loss?

revise.summary: Power delivered to a resistor is P = VI = I²R = V²/R, appearing as heat. Transmission loss is I²Rc = P²Rc/V², so power is sent at very high voltage to cut losses.
traps: In series the higher-wattage bulb does not glow brighter; the lower-wattage (higher R) one does
Don't use minutes in kWh; convert to hours

learn.hook: Why does a car's headlight dim when you crank the starter? The battery's own internal resistance steals voltage when a big current flows.
points: An electrolytic cell has two electrodes in an electrolyte. Its emf ε is the potential difference between its terminals when no current flows.
Every cell has an internal resistance r due to its electrolyte.
With current I drawn through an external resistor R: I = ε/(R + r) and terminal voltage V = ε - Ir = IR.
Terminal voltage is less than ε while the cell is delivering current. Maximum current, on short circuit (R = 0), is ε/r.
Emf is not a force; it is energy supplied per unit charge by the cell (unit: volt).

example.q: A cell of emf 2 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω is connected to a 3.5 Ω resistor. Find I and V.

learn.reallife: Inverter batteries in Indian homes are rated by emf (12 V) and must have low internal resistance so their voltage does not sag badly when the fridge or fan draws current during a power cut.

items.q: ε = 6 V, r = 1 Ω, R = 5 Ω: I (in A)
Same cell: terminal V (in V)
ε = 1.5 V, r = 0.5 Ω: short-circuit I (in A)
ε = 12 V, I = 2 A, r = 0.5 Ω: V (in V)
Open circuit: terminal V equals

quiz.q: A cell of emf 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.3 Ω is connected to a 1.2 Ω resistor. What is the current (in A)?
quiz.mistake: Ignores the internal resistance

quiz.q: A 12 V battery with r = 0.4 Ω supplies 5 A. What is its terminal voltage (in V)?
quiz.mistake: Adds Ir instead of subtracting (that would be charging)

quiz.q: The terminal voltage of a cell is 2.2 V on open circuit and 1.8 V when a current of 2 A flows. What is the internal resistance (in Ω)?
quiz.mistake: Divides the terminal voltage by the current

quiz.q: What is the maximum current that can be drawn from a cell of emf 9 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω (in A)?
quiz.explain: Short circuit: I = ε/r = 9/0.5 = 18 A.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies ε by r

quiz.q: Why is the terminal voltage of a cell less than its emf when it supplies current?
options: Charge is lost inside the cell
Part of the emf is used to drive current through the internal resistance (Ir drop)
The external resistor increases the emf
quiz.explain: V = ε - Ir.
steps: Inside the cell the current passes its internal resistance
Part of ε is used up as Ir, so V = ε − Ir
Answer: Part of the emf is used to drive current through the internal resistance (Ir drop)
quiz.mistake: Thinks the emf itself drops instantly

quiz.q: Emf of a cell is best described as
options: the internal resistance of the cell
the energy supplied per unit charge by the cell, equal to the terminal p.d. on open circuit
quiz.explain: Despite its name, emf is not a force; it is measured in volts.
steps: Emf is energy given per unit charge, measured in volts
It equals the terminal p.d. when no current flows
Answer: the energy supplied per unit charge by the cell, equal to the terminal p.d. on open circuit
quiz.mistake: Takes 'electromotive force' literally

quiz.q: A cell gives 0.5 A through a 4 Ω resistor and 0.25 A through a 9 Ω resistor. What is its emf (in V)?
quiz.mistake: Ignores internal resistance and uses V = IR for one case only

quiz.q: A cell with ε = 2 V, r = 1 Ω is connected to R = 1 Ω. What is the power delivered to R (in W)?
quiz.mistake: Ignores the internal resistance when finding I

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'My 1.5 V cell shows only 1.3 V across the bulb. Is the cell lying?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Some voltage, Ir, is used up inside the cell, so terminal voltage = ε - Ir. Honest cell!
teach.nudge: Good! What is inside a cell that uses up part of its emf when current flows?

revise.summary: A cell's emf ε is its terminal p.d. on open circuit; its internal resistance r causes an Ir drop. With external R, I = ε/(R + r) and V = ε − Ir; the short-circuit current is ε/r.
focus: Finding r and ε from data
traps: Emf is not a force
V equals ε only when no current flows

topics.title: Cells in series and in parallel

learn.hook: A torch uses cells in series for more voltage. Solar panel farms in Rajasthan combine panels in series and parallel to get both voltage and current.
points: Two cells in series (positive of one to negative of the other): ε_eq = ε₁ + ε₂ and r_eq = r₁ + r₂. If one cell is reversed, ε_eq = ε₁ - ε₂ while r_eq still adds.
Two cells in parallel: ε_eq = (ε₁r₂ + ε₂r₁)/(r₁ + r₂) and 1/r_eq = 1/r₁ + 1/r₂.
n identical cells (ε, r) in series: emf nε, resistance nr. m identical cells in parallel: emf ε, resistance r/m.
Mixed grouping (m parallel rows, each of n cells in series): ε_eq = nε and r_eq = nr/m; current I = nε/(R + nr/m).
Series increases voltage; parallel lowers internal resistance and lets more current be drawn.

example.q: Two cells of emf 2 V and 1 V with internal resistances 1 Ω and 2 Ω are joined in parallel. Find ε_eq and r_eq.

learn.reallife: Electric rickshaws on Indian streets typically use four 12 V batteries in series, giving 48 V to drive the motor.

items.q: 4 cells of 1.5 V in series: emf (in V)
4 cells of 1.5 V in parallel: emf (in V)
3 cells, r = 0.6 Ω each, in series: r_eq (in Ω)
3 cells, r = 0.6 Ω each, in parallel: r_eq (in Ω)
Cells of 6 V and 4 V in series, one reversed: emf (in V)

games.title: Grouping rules
items: In series, the internal resistances add.
r_eq = r₁ + r₂.
Reversing one cell in a series pair also subtracts its internal resistance.
Emfs subtract but resistances still add.
Identical cells in parallel have the same emf as a single cell.
ε_eq = ε for identical cells.
Parallel grouping increases the internal resistance.
It decreases it to r/m.
Two parallel cells with ε₁ ≠ ε₂ have an emf between ε₁ and ε₂.
ε_eq is a weighted average.

quiz.q: Two cells of 1.5 V (r = 0.5 Ω each) are in series with a 2 Ω resistor. What is the current (in A)?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to add internal resistances

quiz.q: Cells of emf 6 V (r = 1 Ω) and 2 V (r = 1 Ω) are connected in series with opposite polarity across a 2 Ω resistor. What is the current (in A)?
quiz.mistake: Adds the emfs despite reversed polarity

quiz.q: Two cells of 4 V and 2 V with internal resistances 2 Ω and 2 Ω are connected in parallel. What is the equivalent emf (in V)?
quiz.mistake: Adds the emfs as in series

quiz.q: Six identical cells, each of emf 2 V and internal resistance 0.6 Ω, are arranged as 2 parallel rows of 3 cells in series. What is the internal resistance of the combination (in Ω)?
steps: n = 3 in series per row, m = 2 rows
quiz.mistake: Uses n × r without dividing by the number of rows

quiz.q: For the same arrangement (2 rows of 3 cells of 2 V, 0.6 Ω each) connected to a 5.1 Ω resistor, what is the current (in A)?
quiz.mistake: Takes emf as 12 V by adding all six cells

quiz.q: Four identical cells (ε, r) are connected in parallel. The equivalent emf and internal resistance are
quiz.explain: Identical cells in parallel keep emf ε and divide r by the number of cells.
steps: Identical cells in parallel: emf stays ε
quiz.mistake: Uses the series rule for emf

quiz.q: Why are cells connected in parallel when a large current is needed at low voltage?
options: Parallel grouping reduces the internal resistance, so more current can flow
It makes the cells last a shorter time
quiz.explain: r_eq = r/m drops, raising the maximum current.
steps: Parallel grouping: r_eq = r/m is smaller
Lower internal resistance lets a larger current flow at the same emf
Answer: Parallel grouping reduces the internal resistance, so more current can flow
quiz.mistake: Thinks parallel increases the voltage

quiz.q: Two cells of emf 2 V and 2 V with internal resistances 1 Ω and 3 Ω are in parallel. What is the equivalent internal resistance (in Ω)?
quiz.explain: r_eq = r₁r₂/(r₁ + r₂) = 3/4 = 0.75 Ω.
quiz.mistake: Adds the internal resistances

teach.ask: Gappu has many cells and asks: 'How do I get more voltage? And how do I get more current?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Series adds the emfs for more voltage; parallel lowers internal resistance for more current. Power up!
teach.nudge: Good! Which grouping adds the emfs, and which reduces the internal resistance?

revise.summary: Cells in series add emfs (or subtract if reversed) and internal resistances. In parallel ε_eq = (ε₁r₂ + ε₂r₁)/(r₁ + r₂) and 1/r_eq = 1/r₁ + 1/r₂; m rows of n cells give nε and nr/m.
remember: Series: ε = ε₁ ± ε₂; r = r₁ + r₂
Parallel: ε = (ε₁r₂ + ε₂r₁)/(r₁ + r₂); r = r₁r₂/(r₁ + r₂)
Mixed: ε = nε, r = nr/m; I = nε/(R + nr/m)
traps: Don't subtract r for a reversed cell; only its emf subtracts
Identical cells in parallel do not add emfs; the emf stays ε

learn.hook: Some circuits cannot be reduced to simple series and parallel parts. Gustav Kirchhoff gave two rules that crack any network, from a torch to the national grid.
points: Junction rule: at any junction, the sum of currents entering equals the sum of currents leaving. This is conservation of charge.
Loop rule: the algebraic sum of changes in potential around any closed loop is zero. This is conservation of energy.
Sign convention: going across a resistor in the direction of the assumed current, the potential drops (-IR); against it, it rises (+IR). Going from - to + terminal of a cell, potential rises (+ε).
If a current comes out negative, it simply flows opposite to the direction assumed.
Symmetry helps: in a cube of 12 equal resistors R, the resistance between opposite corners is 5R/6.

example.q: At a junction, 3 A and 2 A flow in along two wires, and 1.5 A flows out along a third. What flows in the fourth wire?
steps: Sum out must also be 5 A
example.answer: 3.5 A flowing out of the junction

learn.reallife: Power engineers at India's National Load Despatch Centre use network equations based on Kirchhoff's rules to balance power flows between regional grids every minute.

games.title: Rule and principle
pairs: Current flows opposite to the assumed direction

games.title: Solving a network
items: Mark an assumed current in each branch
Apply the junction rule at junctions
Choose independent closed loops
Apply the loop rule with sign conventions
Solve the equations and interpret signs

quiz.q: At a junction, currents of 4 A and 3 A enter and a current of 5 A leaves along one wire. What current leaves through the only other wire (in A)?
quiz.explain: In = out: 4 + 3 = 5 + I, so I = 2 A.
steps: Junction rule: total in = total out
quiz.mistake: Adds all currents together

quiz.q: Kirchhoff's loop rule is a consequence of
quiz.explain: A charge that goes round a loop returns to the same potential, so no net energy is gained or lost.
steps: Round a closed loop a charge returns to the same potential
No net energy is gained or lost: conservation of energy
quiz.mistake: Swaps the two rules

quiz.q: In a loop, you go across a 4 Ω resistor in the direction opposite to its current of 2 A. The change in potential is (in V)
quiz.explain: Going against the current, potential rises by IR = +8 V.
steps: Crossing a resistor against the current, potential rises
quiz.mistake: Uses -IR regardless of direction

quiz.q: A single loop has a 10 V cell (negligible r) and resistors of 2 Ω and 3 Ω in series. Using the loop rule, what is the current (in A)?
quiz.mistake: Uses only one resistor

quiz.q: A loop contains a 12 V cell and a 4 V cell connected to oppose each other, with a total resistance of 4 Ω (including internal resistances). What is the current (in A)?
quiz.explain: Net emf = 12 - 4 = 8 V. I = 8/4 = 2 A, in the direction driven by the 12 V cell.
quiz.mistake: Adds the opposing emfs

quiz.q: While solving a network, a current comes out as -0.5 A. This means
options: the current is 0.5 A but flows opposite to the direction assumed
quiz.explain: The assumed direction was just a guess; the sign corrects it.
steps: The direction of current was only assumed
A negative result means it actually flows the other way
Answer: the current is 0.5 A but flows opposite to the direction assumed
quiz.mistake: Thinks a negative current is impossible

quiz.q: Twelve equal resistors of 6 Ω form the edges of a cube. What is the equivalent resistance between two diagonally opposite corners (in Ω)?
quiz.explain: R_eq = 5R/6 = 5 × 6/6 = 5 Ω (by symmetry: current I splits into 3, then 6, then 3 parts).
steps: By symmetry I splits into I/3, then I/6, then I/3
quiz.mistake: Forgets the symmetric splitting of current

quiz.q: Kirchhoff's junction rule is based on
quiz.explain: Charge cannot pile up at a junction in steady state.
steps: Charge cannot pile up at a junction in steady state
So current in = current out: conservation of charge
quiz.mistake: Swaps the two rules

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What are the two Kirchhoff rules, and why are they true?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Junction rule: current in = out (charge conservation). Loop rule: potential changes add to zero (energy conservation). Woohoo!
teach.nudge: Good! What does each rule say, and which conservation law is behind it?

revise.summary: Kirchhoff's junction rule (charge conservation) says current in equals current out; the loop rule (energy conservation) says potential changes round a loop sum to zero. Careful sign conventions and symmetry solve networks.
focus: Interpreting negative currents; cube of resistors
remember: Across R with current: −IR; against: +IR; cell − to +: +ε
Cube of 12 R across body diagonal: 5R/6
traps: A negative current is not an error; it only means the current flows opposite to the direction assumed
Don't mix them up: the loop rule is energy conservation, the junction rule is charge conservation

learn.hook: Before digital meters, the Wheatstone bridge was the gold standard for measuring resistance. It still hides inside weighing scales and strain gauges.
points: Four resistors P, Q, R and S form a diamond ABCD: P from A to B, Q from B to C, R from A to D, S from D to C. A cell is connected across A and C, and a galvanometer across B and D.
Balanced bridge: no current flows through the galvanometer, so B and D are at the same potential.
Applying Kirchhoff's rules with Ig = 0 gives the balance condition P/Q = R/S.
If three resistances are known, the fourth is found from the balance condition: S = RQ/P.
If the bridge is not balanced, a current flows through the galvanometer; it is found using Kirchhoff's rules.

example.q: In a balanced Wheatstone bridge, P = 100 Ω, Q = 10 Ω and R = 30 Ω. Find the unknown S.

learn.reallife: Digital weighing scales at Indian kirana shops use strain gauges in a Wheatstone bridge: the weight slightly changes one arm's resistance, unbalancing the bridge in proportion to the load.

items.text: At balance, the current through the galvanometer is ___.
At balance, points B and D are at the same ___.
A bridge with Ig ≠ 0 is called ___.

items.q: P = 2 Ω, Q = 4 Ω, R = 3 Ω: S (in Ω)
P = 10 Ω, Q = 10 Ω, R = 7 Ω: S (in Ω)
P = 5 Ω, Q = 1 Ω, R = 20 Ω: S (in Ω)
P = 100 Ω, Q = 50 Ω, R = 40 Ω: S (in Ω)
P = 3 Ω, Q = 9 Ω, R = 2 Ω: S (in Ω)

quiz.q: A Wheatstone bridge balances with P = 8 Ω, Q = 2 Ω and R = 12 Ω. What is S (in Ω)?
quiz.explain: P/Q = R/S gives S = RQ/P = 24/8 = 3 Ω.
quiz.mistake: Inverts the ratio and gets 48 Ω

quiz.q: In a balanced bridge, why does no current flow through the galvanometer?
options: The two ends of the galvanometer are at the same potential
The currents in all four arms are equal
quiz.explain: Current flows only if there is a potential difference across the galvanometer.
steps: In balance, B and D are at the same potential
No potential difference ⇒ no galvanometer current
Answer: The two ends of the galvanometer are at the same potential
quiz.mistake: Thinks balance needs all arms to carry equal current

quiz.q: Four resistors P = 2 Ω, Q = 4 Ω, R = 6 Ω and S = 12 Ω form a bridge. Is it balanced?
options: No, since P + Q ≠ R + S
Only if the cell emf is 6 V
quiz.explain: 2/4 = 6/12 = 0.5, so the bridge is balanced whatever the cell.
steps: They are equal, so the bridge is balanced
quiz.mistake: Compares sums instead of ratios

quiz.q: In a balanced bridge, the galvanometer and the cell are interchanged. The bridge
quiz.explain: The condition P/Q = R/S is symmetric; swapping cell and galvanometer keeps balance.
steps: Balance condition P/Q = R/S is symmetric
Interchanging cell and galvanometer leaves it satisfied
quiz.mistake: Thinks positions of cell and galvanometer matter for balance

quiz.q: A bridge has P = Q = R = 10 Ω and S = 10 Ω with a galvanometer of 20 Ω. If S is changed to 20 Ω, will a galvanometer current flow?
options: No, because the galvanometer resistance is large
Only if the cell is reversed
quiz.explain: Balance needs P/Q = R/S; now 1 ≠ 1/2, so the bridge is unbalanced.
steps: 1 ≠ 0.5, so the bridge is unbalanced and current flows
quiz.mistake: Thinks P = Q alone ensures balance

quiz.q: In bridge ABCD, P = 1 Ω (A to B), Q = 2 Ω (B to C), R = 2 Ω (A to D) and S = 1 Ω (D to C). A 10 V cell of negligible internal resistance is connected across A and C, and a galvanometer of resistance 2 Ω across B and D. What current flows through the galvanometer (in A)?
quiz.explain: P/Q = 1/2 but R/S = 2, so the bridge is unbalanced. Taking V_C = 0 and V_A = 10 V, the junction rule at B and D gives V_B = 6 V and V_D = 4 V, so Ig = (6 - 4)/2 = 1 A, from B to D.
quiz.mistake: Assumes the galvanometer current is zero without checking the balance condition

quiz.q: When a bridge is balanced, the galvanometer can be removed without changing any current. Why?
options: Because it is in series with the cell
It carries zero current, so removing it changes nothing
quiz.explain: A branch with zero current can be removed (or replaced by any resistor) without effect.
steps: At balance the galvanometer branch carries zero current
Removing a zero-current branch changes nothing
Answer: It carries zero current, so removing it changes nothing
quiz.mistake: Thinks every branch affects the network

quiz.q: In a balanced bridge P = 4 Ω, Q = 6 Ω and S = 9 Ω. What is R (in Ω)?
quiz.mistake: Rearranges the balance condition wrongly

quiz.q: A wire of resistance 8 Ω is used as S in a balanced bridge with P = 2 Ω and Q = 4 Ω. What is R (in Ω)?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies all three resistances

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What is so special about a balanced Wheatstone bridge?'
teach.praise: Chirp! At balance the galvanometer shows zero current because its ends are at the same potential, and P/Q = R/S. Bridge mastered!
teach.nudge: Good! What does the galvanometer show at balance, and what condition holds?

revise.summary: A Wheatstone bridge has four resistors with a cell and a galvanometer across opposite corners. At balance no galvanometer current flows and P/Q = R/S, giving an unknown resistance; otherwise Kirchhoff's rules find the current.
remember: At balance the galvanometer branch can be removed
traps: Don't compare the ratios in the wrong order; match P/Q with R/S
Swapping the cell and galvanometer does not upset the balance
